sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
Take the descent lemma and aim it at a pure gradient step. The new point is the old point minus \(t\) times the gradient. The displacement is \(-t \nabla f\), so the linear term in the upper bound is \(-t\) times the squared gradient norm. The quadratic penalty contributes \((L/2) t^2\) times the same squared norm. Subtracting the upper bound from the old value produces a guaranteed decrease of \(t(1 - L t/2)\) times \(\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\).

The coefficient is positive exactly when the step lies strictly between zero and \(2/L\). At the right endpoint the guarantee drops to zero. Past that endpoint the algebra no longer promises a decrease, and a long gradient step can diverge. Among the constant steps inside the interval, the coefficient \(t - (L/2) t^2\) is a downward parabola. Its maximum is at \(t = 1/L\), where the decrease is at least the squared gradient norm divided by \(2L\).

The same decrease is an Armijo certificate. Along the negative gradient, Armijo with parameter \(c\) asks for a decrease of at least \(c t\) times the squared norm. The lemma meets that request whenever \(1 - L t/2\) is at least \(c\), which is the step restriction \(t \le 2(1 - c)/L\). Backtracking can therefore stop: a short enough trial is not merely acceptable in the limit, it is covered by an explicit bound.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For \(0 < t < 2/L\),
\[
f(x) - f(x - t \nabla f(x)) \ge t\Bigl(1 - \frac{L t}{2}\Bigr) \lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2.
\]
At \(t = 1/L\) the coefficient equals \(1/(2L)\). Armijo with parameter \(c\) holds for \(t \le 2(1 - c)/L\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(L = 6\), take the step \(t = 1/6\), and let the squared gradient norm be \(36\). This step is \(1/L\). The coefficient is \((1/6)(1 - 6 \cdot (1/6) / 2) = (1/6)(1/2) = 1/12\). Multiply by the squared norm.

The ramp drop is 3. The lemma promises that the objective falls by at least \(3\), whatever the rest of \(f\) looks like, as long as the Lipschitz constant really is \(6\). The boundary step \(2/L = 1/3\) would have promised a drop of zero. A step of \(1/L\) is the constant choice that makes the promise as large as this argument allows.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Adding the quadratic term instead of subtracting it replaces \(1 - L t/2\) by \(1 + L t/2\) and invents a decrease that the upper bound does not give. A second slip is to call \(t = 2/L\) a strict decrease. The coefficient there is zero. A third is to maximize the coefficient at \(t = 2/L\). The vertex of the parabola is at half of that, \(t = 1/L\). A fourth is to match Armijo with \(c = 1\) for a positive step. The rearrangement \(t \le 2(1 - c)/L\) collapses to \(t \le 0\) when \(c = 1\). The lemma does not promise the full linear prediction.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Summing the inequality over many steps bounds the sum of the squared gradient norms by the gap in the objective. That sum is the start of the convergence proof for the gradient method. The same decrease survives projection onto a convex set when the projection does not increase distances, which is why a projected gradient step can quote this lemma with the same \(L\).
